extras.description: Artist-published Elixir (2015) credits the complete album union: Jose Conde lead voice, maracas, guiro and coros; Obanilu Ire congas, pandero, shakers, guayo, agogo and coros; Gabriel Machado timbales, bongos, congas and campana; Rey David Alejandre, John Speck and Jose Davila trombones; Dennis Hernandez trumpet; Pablo Vergara piano; Jorge Bringas bass and coros; Juan Carlos Formell bass; Roberto Quintero conga dos, tumbador, maracas, guiro and campana; Roman Diaz quinto and claves. Artist publishes explicit modern-salsa classification and describes progressive Brooklyn salsa dura with Cuban son/timba roots. Whole nine-track album union, including all guests and named auxiliary percussion; not an assertion every role is simultaneous on every track. Three named singers are retained (Conde, Ire, Bringas); no other credited musician is guessed to sing. Separate pandero, shaker, guayo and agogo owners preserve named identities with unspecified construction. Multi-register conga owner preserves quinto/conga/tumbador roles; separate timbales owner prevents inappropriate hand-slap defaults. Bass is credited without construction; electric bass is an explicit authored realization of the bass-family role, not claimed source hardware. Authored steel timbales, oak/mule-hide congas and bongos, gourd/seed maracas, Cuban guiro, welded campana, rosewood Son 3-2 claves, unmuted punchy Bb trumpet/tenor trombone, fingerstyle bass and Steinway D9ft jazz comping provide a coherent model; exact materials, clave orientation and gestures are not measured from the source. tradition.name: Música Andina Colombiana
tradition.lineage: Guafa Trío — complete host-published 29 September 2016 Texas State touring ensemble palette. Authored present-day recording arrangement based on the documented selected performance branch. Sources support category, credited roles and locality. Materials, makes, technique presets, tuning, studio, signal chain and axes are authored realizations, not measured historical session settings or universal genre rules.

extras.description: University concert presenter specifies cuatro and maracas, transverse flute, and both acoustic and electric bass. Ignacio Ramos is flute/maracas specialist; Cristian Camilo Guataquira is cuatro llanero player; Javier Andrés Mesa Martínez is bassist. All five instrumental families across three performers are retained. Creator-owned Música Andina Colombiana playlist includes Guafa Trío Bambuquísimo at item7. Booking-agent WOMEX historical profile explicitly describes instrumental music with flute, double bass and cuatro, corroborating the acoustic bass family; it does not replace the broader 2016 host roster. Complete documented touring palette associated with the 2016 hosted recital, rather than an invented flute-only trio or a single unattributed excerpt. Acoustic and electric bass are retained as alternate capabilities of one bassist, and flute/maracas as one player’s alternate roles: not five simultaneous musicians. No singer is named in the complete instrumental ensemble; vocalist collaborations and the expanded 2026 ethnic-percussion palette are separate scopes. The source identifies central/eastern Colombian traditions and orchestral/jazz instruments, and the current government festival confirms improvisation over Andean and llanero rhythmic frames; improvOnFrame represents this documented instrumental elaboration, not all Colombian Andean songs. This regional umbrella remains distinct from the nationwide instrumental umbrella, joropo and pan-Andean indigenous music; no equivalence claim. Cuatro venezolano is the existing four-string shared Colombia/Venezuela llanero instrument, not Puerto Rican ten-string cuatro. Reentrant nylon tuning, cedar construction and rasgueo, seed-filled gourd maracas, silver concert flute, pizzicato double bass and fingerstyle electric bass are authored concrete configurations, not measurements of the 2016 instruments. Bow/rosin inventory does not imply bowing under the pinned pizzicato approach. Authored present-day recording arrangement based on the documented selected performance branch. Sources support category, credited roles and locality. Materials, makes, technique presets, tuning, studio, signal chain and axes are authored realizations, not measured historical session settings or universal genre rules.

Three alternate instrument families across two musicians, no singer; metaphorical musical voices in the promotional text are not literal vocal credits. Cello and violin are Guallar’s alternate roles, not an invented simultaneous string section. The program is not the full studio albums, which can include further guest instruments and overdubs. Distinct from Aragón jota, rock and pan-European bal-folk through the positive regional category and precisely scoped member program. extras.description: Artist-owned single gives all performance credits: Lucas Moura voice and acoustic guitar, Lucas and Zé Nigro backing vocals, João Boaventura electric piano, Zé synthesizer, Thiago Leal bass, Pedro Lacerda drums, Fernando Bastos transverse flute. Two distinct vocalists across six musicians, not three singers merely because Lucas has two vocal credits. Same complete credits recur on the album track. Creator-owned Música Campista playlist includes Glue Trip at items23 and88. Artist-owned biography identifies João Pessoa base; category membership does not imply Campos birth or residence. The complete independently released single provides a non-arbitrary arrangement boundary. All seven families and both singers retained, including guest flute and electric piano; album-wide guests Arthur Verocai, YMA, Otto and Felipe S are not silently imported into this separately credited song. FunctionalSong is an authored verse/refrain plus functional-chord arrangement compatible with the published recurring lyric sections and psychedelic-pop tags, not a claimed measured harmonic transcription. This realization represents one positive creator-member branch, not all Campista music, João Pessoa indie or Brazilian synthpop. Source acoustic guitar is realized as fingerpicked steel-string OM, unspecified electric piano as mellow tine piano with restrained tremolo, unspecified synth as five-voice Prophet-type pad, unspecified bass as fingerstyle electric bass and transverse flute as silver concert flute. These are disclosed production choices, not measured artist gear, materials or exact techniques. One featured lead with accompanying vocal overdubs is represented by the solo-accompanied foreground and an authored lead/third/fifth recording stack. Three recorded harmonic lanes do not mean three singers: only Lucas and Zé are credited; exact source intervals are not claimed. The credited double bass is realized pizzicato consistently in both bass_play and bowed technique; handclaps use a group setting. No additional theater instruments are inferred. extras.description: Artist labels the track a chilena oaxaqueña and explicitly identifies its verses as adapted traditional coplas from Costa Chica, Oaxaca. Track-specific credits name Augusto Bracho voice/guitarra criolla; Pablo Navarro double bass/backing voice; Martín Bruhn percussion/backing voice/claps; Marina Sorín cello/backing voice/claps; Diego Galaz horn violin; Jorge Arribas accordion; and Romelia Granados plus Nacho Mastretta backing voices/claps. Regional Oaxaca repertoire is broader than this adapted Costa Chica copla/chilena realization; the track is not equated to all Oaxaca music or to unaltered traditional performance. Complete track credits retain all eight sound families and six named singers, including backing voices and handclaps. The credited violín trompeta is a horn-amplified violin, not a separate brass trumpet; primary broadcaster documentation of Galaz calls the instrument stroviol. Generic percussion remains the neutral credited-auxiliary owner. Nylon guitar, coherent arco bass plus local-song bowing for all three bowed-string families, piano accordion construction and group claps are explicitly authored choices, not measured source techniques or construction. Mexican song-family parent follows the adapted regional copla verses and full strings/accordion ensemble, without a narrower corrido or ranchera claim. Oaxaca city is an editorial state-repertoire anchor, not the Costa Chica recording site or birthplace claim. tradition.lineage: Amancia Pérez and ensemble — Sarandunga (1976 Folkways release, Baní field recording). Representative authored present-day recording arrangement for the selected documented branch. Sources establish category, roles and locality. Exact materials, makes, playing settings, tuning, room, signal chain and axes are authored choices, not measured source-session facts or universal genre characteristics.

extras.description: Smithsonian track credits and producer liner notes name Amancia Pérez as singer, Carlos Enriques, Raphael Peguero and Carlos Peguero on three tamboras, and Manuel Ventura on metal güiro. The selected recording comprises Bomba and Jacana dance sections in the local Sarandunga feast honoring St John the Baptist. Liner notes identify Baní and explicitly describe barrel-shaped two-headed drums struck with hand and stick, plus metal scraper and metal stick. Complete named five-person selected field-recording ensemble, with three tambora players aggregated in one family card and one positively credited singer. Wider procession/community singing is contextual and is not imported as unnamed additional recorded singers. Percussion-led ritual dances justify groovePercussion; this national traditional umbrella is broader than merengue and bachata and no equivalence is asserted. Existing tambora hand-and-stick geometry matches primary description; avocado shell and skin construction are transparent authored defaults, not measured source facts. Isolated metal-güiro owner avoids falsely imposing the existing merengue/bachata pattern vocabulary on Sarandunga. No drum-machine, guitar or additional voices from neighboring album tracks imported. extras.description: Artist release credits Noura Mint Seymali lead voice and ardin, Jeiche Ould Chighaly guitar, Matthew C. Tinari drums, Ousmane Touré bass, and Mayassa Hemed Vall backing voice. Full five-person, two-singer ensemble retained; artist and recording identify Nouakchott, Mauritania. The Mauritanian national category is broader than this documented Moorish modal electric-band realization and is not equivalent to Mande kora praise singing. First-person interview explicitly says Azawan II follows a Moorish modal order, incompletely, and the Azawan approach removed Western-tuned guitar/keyboards to free the Moorish melodic guitar. This supports the modal-electric placement; no Western harmonic progression or literal continuous drone is claimed. Complete EP credits retained without importing tidinite or wedding percussion from other practice descriptions. Authored humbucker guitar, overdriven single-note lead, open-D tuning and equal temperament are transparent modern realization choices, not measurements or transcription of Jeiche’s Moorish tuning; no invented actual gear. The two vocal performers use an authored duet arrangement without claiming a live simultaneous take. Representative authored present-day recording arrangement for the selected documented branch.
